reason: The molecule (C5H9N3O) is essentially ethylamino-cyanoacetamide: CH3-CH2-NH(3)-CH(5)(C≡N)(6,7)-C(=O)(9,10)-NH2(11,12,13). Its conformational energy is dominated by (a) formation of a favorable intramolecular H-bond stabilizing a 5-membered pseudo-ring, either the secondary-amine N3-H4 donating to the amide carbonyl O10 (ring N3-C5-C9-O10...H4) or the amide N11-H12 donating to the amine nitrogen N3 (ring N11-C9-C5-N3...H12), and (b) avoidance of steric/eclipsing clashes in the ethyl and cyanomethine backbone. I measured the relevant donor-acceptor distances (H4···O10 and H12/H13···N3, and as weaker alternatives H···N7 of the nitrile) across all 30 conformers. Distances in the 2.10-2.30 Å range indicate a well-formed, close-to-linear intramolecular H-bond typical of a 5-membered turn; distances >2.5 Å indicate the donor/acceptor pair is present but poorly aligned or too far to contribute meaningful stabilization; and conformers where neither classic interaction is close (best contact >2.7-3.9 Å, e.g. 28, 12, 3, 23, 9) are judged least stabilized, relying only on weak, long-range electrostatics or the weaker amide-to-nitrile contact. Using the shortest qualifying H-bond distance found in each conformer as the primary stability proxy (shorter = more stabilizing, all else being roughly comparable since the heavy-atom connectivity and rotatable bonds are identical), I ranked the conformers from tightest/most linear intramolecular H-bond to essentially H-bond-free extended conformations. Conformers 27, 30, 19 and 7 show the shortest, best-aligned N-H···N(amine) contacts (~2.10-2.12 Å); 18, 25, 15, 14, 13 show strong N-H···O=C contacts or comparable N-H···N contacts (2.15-2.18 Å); a middle group (22, 29, 20, 1, 5, 10, 26, 24, 4, 6, 11) shows moderate H-bonding (2.19-2.33 Å); a lower group (21, 17, 16, 2, 8) shows only weak/long H-bond geometry (2.39-2.50 Å); and the bottom group (9, 23, 3, 12, 28) lacks any close, well-aligned intramolecular H-bond (best contacts 2.7-3.9 Å), making them the least stabilized, extended/open conformations. This ranking is approximate—true relative energies would require full QM optimization/energy evaluation—but the H-bond geometry criterion, combined with the absence of obvious severe steric clashes in the top-ranked structures, provides a chemically reasonable ordering. Greatest uncertainty lies in the middle of the list where H-bond distances are closely spaced (differences of only 0.01-0.05 Å) and could be reordered by more subtle secondary steric effects not captured by a single distance metric.

This molecule is ethyl alaninate: CH3CH2-O-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-NH2 (C1..C2 ethyl, O5 ester/ether O, C6 carbonyl C, O7 carbonyl O, C8 alpha-C, N9 amino N, C12 alpha-methyl). The main conformational degree of freedom that differentiates stability is rotation about the Cα-C(=O) bond (N9-C8-C6-O7 dihedral), which determines whether the NH2 group can form a short intramolecular contact/weak H-bond to the carbonyl oxygen (O7, a good H-bond acceptor, sp2 lone pairs) or instead points toward the ester (ether) oxygen O5 (a weaker acceptor). 

Measuring N9...O7 distances across all conformers gives a clear bimodal split: ~2.78 Å (NH2 oriented toward carbonyl O) versus ~3.44-3.64 Å (NH2 rotated away from carbonyl O). In the short-distance group, I checked which amine H (H10/H11) is closest to O7: conformers 2, 5, 6, 20, 21, 23 show one N-H...O7 distance of ~2.35-2.36 Å, indicating a fairly well-aligned weak intramolecular N-H...O=C hydrogen bond (5-membered ring N-Cα-C=O...H), which is stabilizing. Conformers 1, 3, 17, 26, 29, 30 also have short N...O7 (~2.78-2.79 Å) but with both N-H...O7 distances only moderate (~2.6-2.85 Å), i.e. the NH2 lone-pair/dipole is oriented near the carbonyl but the H-bond geometry is less optimal — these are still favorable but somewhat less so than the first group.

For the conformers where NH2 points away from the carbonyl (long N...O7), I checked contacts to the ether oxygen O5 instead. Most of these show a secondary weak N-H...O5 interaction. Conformers 7, 25, 12, 28 have the best of these (H...O5 ~2.33-2.35 Å), while 11, 18, 10, 13, 8, 16, 24, 9, 14, 4, 15, 19, 27, 22 have progressively weaker/looser H...O5 contacts (~2.46-2.52 Å). Because carbonyl oxygen is a stronger H-bond acceptor than the ester (ether-type) oxygen, conformers that engage NH2 with the carbonyl oxygen are ranked above those that only engage the weaker ether oxygen, even when the ether-oxygen geometry is quantitatively tighter, though this ordering between the two families is the most uncertain part of the ranking given the overall small energy differences expected for rotamers of a small flexible amino-ester. No severe steric clashes (short heavy-atom or H...H contacts <2.0 Å) were found in any conformer, so differences are all subtle, second-order (H-bond quality/dipole alignment) effects rather than gross strain differences.

The molecule (CH3-C≡C-CH2-O-CH2-CH(OH)-CH3, atoms in fixed order C1..C4, O5(ether), C6, C7, O8(hydroxyl), H9(OH-H), C9(methyl)...) has a rigid alkyne (C2≡C3, bond length ~1.2 Å) flanking a flexible -CH2-O-CH2-CH(OH)-CH3 chain. The dominant stabilizing interaction available to this chain is an intramolecular hydrogen bond in which the hydroxyl H (atom 9) reaches back to the ether oxygen (atom 5), forming a favorable 5-membered pseudo-ring (O5-C6-C7-O8-H9...O5). This kind of H-bond is well known to stabilize glycol-ether-type fragments by several kcal/mol when the O...H distance is ~2.2-2.4 Å with reasonable O-H...O alignment; when the OH rotates away (O...H distance > 2.7 Å, and especially > 3.4 Å) the stabilization is lost and the conformer is a simple extended/gauche chain without compensating H-bonding, which should generally raise its relative energy.

I measured the O5(ether)...H9(hydroxyl) distance in every conformer (same atom ordering/connectivity in all files). This clearly splits the 30 conformers into two groups: (A) 13 conformers with O...H ≈ 2.20-2.34 Å, consistent with an intact/near-optimal intramolecular H-bond, and (B) 17 conformers with O...H ≈ 2.78-4.4 Å, where the OH is rotated away and no meaningful H-bond exists. Within group A, I rank by increasing O...H distance (shorter/more linear-looking H-bond assumed more stabilizing): conformers 2, 13, 7, 24 are essentially tied at the shortest distances (~2.20-2.21 Å), followed by 26, 19, 3, 28, 18 (~2.28-2.30 Å), then 11, 14, 16, 27 (~2.33-2.34 Å) which are slightly longer/more strained H-bond geometries (likely slightly non-ideal dihedral alignment increasing torsional strain elsewhere to accommodate the H-bond).

Within group B, none have a real intramolecular H-bond, so ranking is based on how close the geometry still is to reforming one (residual weak dipole stabilization, e.g., 17, 25, 30 at ~2.78-2.79 Å are borderline/weakly interacting) versus fully extended anti conformers where the OH points completely away from the ether oxygen (many conformers cluster near ~3.9-3.95 Å, and two extreme outliers, 10 and 1, are essentially maximally splayed at >4.3 Å, likely reflecting additional unfavorable steric/torsional arrangement along the chain, e.g. eclipsing near the propargylic CH2 or the O-CH2 linkage). These very long-distance conformers are placed at the bottom of the ranking.

This ranking rule (H-bond distance as the dominant stability descriptor) is the most robust geometric signal extractable from the coordinates given the flexible acyclic backbone and rigid alkyne core; finer distinctions within each tier (e.g., between 2 and 13, or between mid-3.9 Å conformers) are less certain and could in principle be reordered by secondary steric effects (gauche vs anti about C3-C4-O5-C6, methyl orientation on C7, etc.) that were not exhaustively quantified here. This introduces some uncertainty in the exact internal ordering within each tier, though the overall two-tier separation (H-bonded vs non-H-bonded) should be reliable.

The molecule (C7H14O2, DoU=1) is a cyclopropane ring (C12/C13/C14) bearing an OH on C12, fused to a CH(OH) center (C11) that also carries an isopropyl group (C5 with two methyls C1,C6). The two OH groups (O19-H20 on the cyclopropane carbon, O21-H22 on the adjacent CH) sit on neighboring carbons (C12-C11), so the dominant conformational energy term is whether they can form a 5-membered intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bond (favorable when the O...H distance is ~2.0-2.4 Å) versus conformers where free rotation about the C11-C12 and C11-C5 bonds points the two OH groups away from each other (O...H distances >3.5 Å, no H-bond, only weak dipole/steric effects). 

For each conformer I computed the two possible intramolecular donor-acceptor distances (H20...O21 and H22...O19) and took the shorter one as the effective H-bond metric. This cleanly splits the 30 conformers into two groups: (i) 16 conformers with a real, though weak-to-moderate, intramolecular H-bond (H...O ≈ 2.0-2.7 Å), and (ii) 14 conformers with no such interaction (H...O ≈ 3.5-4.3 Å), where the two hydroxyls point in unrelated directions and stability is governed mainly by avoidance of steric clashes between the bulky isopropyl group and the cyclopropane ring/OH hydrogens.

Within the H-bonded group, conformer 6 shows the shortest H...O contact (2.04 Å, H22 pointing at O19) combined with a reasonable O-O separation (2.66 Å) consistent with a well-formed 5-membered chelate ring, making it the most stable. Conformers 25, 14, 17, 5, 21, 18, 3, 11, 30, 4, 26, 2, 27, 20 and 9 follow in order of increasing H...O distance (weaker but still stabilizing interactions, 2.1-2.7 Å). 

The non-hydrogen-bonded group (7,1,29,15,8,19,22,13,12,23,16,24,28,10) is ranked by the same residual (weak) donor-acceptor proximity, since even without a formal H-bond, closer heteroatom approach correlates with generally more compact/gauche conformations and slightly lower electrostatic repulsion between the two C-O dipoles; conformers with the largest O...H separations (e.g. 28, 10) also show the most extended, anti arrangements of the isopropyl/cyclopropane/OH groups, which is not obviously stabilizing given the lack of compensating H-bond, so they are placed lowest.

Caveat/uncertainty: this ranking is dominated by the intramolecular H-bond proxy; second-order steric effects (eclipsing of isopropyl methyls with cyclopropane C-H's, cyclopropane ring pucker strain) were not exhaustively checked for every conformer and could shift the ordering within each group by a few positions, especially among the closely spaced middle-ranked structures (H...O ≈ 2.3-2.7 Å) and among the non-H-bonded tail (H...O ≈ 3.8-4.3 Å) where differences are likely within thermal noise.

The molecule is an N-substituted aziridine: the ring nitrogen (atom6) bears a CH(CH2CH3)(CH2OCH3) substituent at the central carbon C3 (atom5). The aziridine ring itself (N-C4-C5, atoms 6,7,8) has fixed, conformer-independent ring strain, so it does not differentiate the 30 conformers. The main conformational variable that can be extracted reliably from the coordinates is the torsion about the O-CH2-CH(N)- fragment, i.e. the dihedral O(14)-C6(13)-C3(5)-N(6). This is the classic 1,2-heteroatom 'gauche effect' motif (analogous to O-C-C-N in aminoethanol ethers), where a ~60° (gauche) arrangement is stabilized by lp(N)->sigma*(C-O)/lp(O)->sigma*(C-N) hyperconjugation relative to the ~180° (anti) arrangement.

I computed this dihedral indirectly via the N...O through-space distance (a reliable proxy since bond lengths/angles are essentially constant): gauche conformations cluster near N...O ~2.9-3.2 Å (dihedral ~55-65°, confirmed explicitly for conformers 21 and 8, ~61° and ~65°), while anti conformations cluster near N...O ~3.5-3.8 Å (confirmed explicitly for conformer 16, ~174°). This produces a clean bimodal split into 18 'gauche' conformers (expected to be stabilized by the gauche effect) and 12 'anti' conformers (expected to lose this stabilization, all else being roughly comparable since ring strain is constant and no classical H-bond donors are present to override this effect).

Within each group, fine energetic ordering is harder to establish rigorously by hand (it would depend on secondary factors such as ethyl-chain staggering about C3-C2, OMe staggering about C6-O-C7, and the rotational alignment of the rigid aziridine ring relative to the bulky ethyl/methoxymethyl substituents on C3, avoiding eclipsing interactions). Lacking a full force-field evaluation, I used the deviation of the N...O distance from the ideal gauche/anti value as a weak secondary tie-breaker (smaller deviation ~ closer to ideal geometry, presumably slightly better optimized), while acknowledging this is a much less certain criterion than the primary gauche-vs-anti classification. Overall confidence: the gauche/anti split (top 18 vs bottom 12) is the most defensible part of this ranking; the ordering within each block is uncertain and should be treated as approximate/tentative.

The molecule is a cyclopropane bearing two hydroxyls (on the carbon also carrying a CH2-C(=O)-CH3 acetonyl chain, and on the adjacent ring CH) plus a ketone carbonyl. The connectivity is identical in all 30 files (atoms 3=C=O oxygen, 10/11=one OH, 15/16=the other OH), so conformers differ mainly in rotamer state of the two O-H groups and the acetonyl chain, which determines whether an intramolecular O-H...O=C (or O-H...OH) hydrogen bond can form. I computed the four possible donor-acceptor H···O distances for every conformer (H11-O3, H11-O15, H16-O3, H16-O10) and used the shortest one as the primary stability descriptor, since a short, well-aligned intramolecular H-bond (H···O ≈ 1.9-2.1 Å) is the dominant stabilizing interaction available in this small polyhydroxy-ketone, while conformers whose OH hydrogens point away from any acceptor (all distances >3.5 Å) lack this stabilization and are judged least stable. Ring strain from the cyclopropane is essentially conformer-independent (same connectivity/stereochemistry throughout), so it does not differentiate the set. Within each H-bonding tier, ordering is by decreasing H-bond quality (shorter H···O = stronger, more stabilizing). This is a reasonable proxy given the data, but subtle differences among conformers with similar H-bond distances (e.g., 9 vs 4, or the whole 'no H-bond' tail group) are uncertain because secondary steric contacts (CH3/ring clashes, gauche vs anti chain orientation) were not exhaustively scanned for every pair.

All 30 conformers share the same skeleton: CH3-CH(OH)-CH(CHO)-C(=O)-CH3 (atoms 3=CHOH carbon bearing O4-H5 hydroxyl, 7=central CH branch point, 8=aldehyde carbon C8=O9 with H10, 11=ketone carbon C11=O12 flanked by methyl C13). The dominant conformational stabilization available to this molecule is an intramolecular O-H(hydroxyl, atom5)...O=C hydrogen bond, which can close either a 6-membered ring to the aldehyde oxygen (O9) or to the ketone oxygen (O12), since both carbonyl carbons are one bond removed from the branch carbon C7 that bears the CH(OH) group. I therefore computed, for every conformer, the through-space distance from the hydroxyl H (atom 5) to both carbonyl oxygens (atom 9 and atom 12) and took the shorter of the two as a proxy for intramolecular H-bond strength (shorter distance ≈ stronger, more linear H-bond, more stabilized conformer; distances below ~2.3 Å indicate a real H-bond, 2.3–3.5 Å indicate weak/distorted interaction, and >4 Å indicate no meaningful interaction, i.e. the OH is rotated away from both carbonyls into a non-bonded orientation that leaves the polar groups unstabilized and often exposed to solvent-free, gauche/eclipsed steric penalties instead).

Ranking obtained (ascending H···O distance, most stable first):
17 (1.92 Å, to ketone O12) and 4 (2.01 Å, ketone) / 15 (2.01 Å, aldehyde) / 10 (2.05 Å, ketone) form the strongest, near-ideal 6-membered-ring H-bonds and are placed at the top.
Conformers 18, 29, 24, 23, 22, 14, 5, 21 show good-to-moderate H-bonds (2.1–2.25 Å) to either O9 or O12 and follow next.
Conformers 13, 27, 28, 9, 20, 11, 25, 8 show only weak, geometrically distorted proximity (3.0–3.8 Å) that provides little real stabilization.
The remaining conformers (3, 19, 6, 16, 12, 7, 2, 26, 30, 1) show no meaningful O-H···O=C contact (>4 Å); in these the hydroxyl is oriented away from both carbonyls, leaving the polar C=O and O-H groups unstabilized and likely accompanied by more eclipsed/gauche torsional strain around the C3-C7 and C7-C11/C7-C8 bonds, so these are ranked as least stable.

Uncertainty: this ranking uses H-bond geometry as the dominant discriminator; secondary effects (methyl-methyl steric clashes, exact torsional eclipsing, dipole–dipole alignment between the aldehyde and ketone carbonyls) were not exhaustively modeled and could shift the order among conformers with similar H-bond distances (e.g., the near-tied pairs 24/23, 5/21, 3/19, 22/14). The relative order within the 'no H-bond' tail (ranks ~21-30) is especially uncertain since all show negligible polar stabilization and differences there are likely small and dominated by torsional strain not directly quantified here.

The 30 conformers share an aromatic 2,5-disubstituted-1H-pyrrole core (N10-C6-C7-C8-C9, ring C-C/C-N distances ~1.36-1.41 Å in every file), with an N-H, an ethyl group on C6 (C5-C1), and a hydroxymethyl group on C9 (C12-O15-H16). Because the ring is aromatic and essentially planar/rigid in all files, the conformational (and energetic) differences between structures come almost entirely from rotamer choices of the two flexible side chains: (1) rotation of the ethyl group about C6-C5, and (2) rotation of the CH2OH group about C9-C12 and C12-O15, which controls whether the hydroxyl oxygen can approach the polarized N-H proton (a weak intramolecular N-H···O electrostatic/H-bond contact) or whether it points away, and whether either substituent clashes with adjacent ring C-H's (H17 on C8, H18 on C7) or with each other across the ring.

I measured the H11(N-H)···O15 distance (and the corresponding N10···O15 distance and N-H-O angle) as the main discriminating metric, since N-H is the only good donor and the alcohol O is the only good acceptor available intramolecularly (the pyrrole N lone pair is delocalized into the ring and is a poor acceptor, so O-H···N is not favorable, but N-H···O is reasonable).

Two conformers, 12 and 20, stand out with a markedly short H11···O15 distance (~2.41 Å, N···O ~2.70 Å) while keeping the ethyl group far from the hydroxymethyl group (no compensating steric clash) — this is consistent with a real, if moderately bent (~95-96°), stabilizing N-H···O intramolecular contact, making these two the most stable.

The remaining 28 conformers show no such close contact; H11···O15 ranges broadly from ~3.0 Å to ~4.1 Å with unfavorable N-H-O angles (checked explicitly for one case, ~82°), indicating essentially no directed electrostatic stabilization, only incidental proximity. For these, I used the residual (weak) trend that a somewhat closer, better-aligned O to the polar N-H region is mildly more favorable than a fully extended/anti arrangement where the CH2OH group points completely away, while spot-checking several members (e.g. conformer 23) for absence of steric clashes between the CH2OH hydrogens and the adjacent ring C-H (H17) or between the ethyl group and H18 — none of the checked structures show short (<2.0-2.3 Å) non-bonded contacts, implying that differences among this majority group are small (likely <1-2 kcal/mol) and this ranking tier is the least certain part of the analysis.

Structures with the most extended arrangement (H11···O15 ≈ 4.09-4.11 Å; e.g. 4, 1, 14, 9, 15, 30, 10, 22) are placed lowest as they gain no stabilizing polar contact and represent the most 'isolated'/dangling hydroxyl rotamers, though I flag that these could in principle be nearly isoenergetic with the mid-tier group given the small magnitude of the effects being resolved by geometry alone.

All 30 conformers share the same connectivity: a central carbinol carbon C5 bearing a methyl group (C1), a hydroxyl (O6-H7), a -CH2-CHO arm (C8-C9=O10, H11 on the aldehyde carbon), and a -CH2-C≡CH arm (C14-C15≡C16-H17). Because the molecule is acyclic and fully saturated except for the terminal alkyne (which is linear and essentially strain-free and conformationally inert about its own axis), the dominant source of differential stability among conformers is not classical ring-strain or eclipsing within a ring, but (1) the possibility of an intramolecular O-H(hydroxyl)···O=C(aldehyde) hydrogen bond across the C5-C8-C9 backbone (forming a favorable 6-membered pseudo-ring: H7-O6-C5-C8-C9=O10), and (2) minor steric/gauche effects in the open-chain arrangement otherwise.

I measured the H7···O10 distance and the O6-H7···O10 angle in every conformer. Six conformers show a short H···O contact (1.9-2.2 Å) with a reasonably favorable donor-H···acceptor angle (128-141°), consistent with a genuine stabilizing intramolecular H-bond: conformer 1 (1.94 Å, 141°, the best-aligned and shortest, hence most stabilized), conformer 16 (2.07 Å, 133°), conformer 2 (2.08 Å, 132°), conformer 6 (2.11 Å, 130°), conformer 21 (2.12 Å, 129°), conformer 26 (2.14 Å, 128°). These should be markedly more stable than the rest because an intramolecular O-H···O=C hydrogen bond to an aldehyde typically contributes a few kcal/mol of stabilization, and no severe steric penalty is required to attain this geometry (the arms simply rotate into a favorable gauche/folded arrangement without any bad eclipsing, since the molecule has no ring constraints).

All remaining 24 conformers show H7···O10 distances of 3.3-5.5 Å with no favorable donor-acceptor alignment, i.e., the hydroxyl and carbonyl point away from each other and no intramolecular H-bond is possible; these conformers are essentially isoenergetic extended/rotated forms differing mainly in minor gauche vs anti placement of the two side arms around the quaternary-like C5 center and in methyl/alkyne orientation, none of which produces large steric clashes because the substituents (CH3, CH2CHO, CH2C≡CH, OH) are modest in size and the alkyne terminus is thin and linear. For these, I used the residual O6-H7···O10 distance as a weak secondary indicator of relative electrostatic/dipole alignment (shorter residual distance ~ somewhat more favorable dipole packing even without a true H-bond), giving a tentative internal ordering, but I flag this tail ordering as having low confidence since true energy differences among these 24 are likely small (sub-1-2 kcal/mol) and not reliably resolvable from geometry alone without QM optimization/energies.

Overall: conformers with a real intramolecular OH···O=C hydrogen bond (1, 16, 2, 6, 21, 26) are placed at the top, ordered by H-bond distance/angle quality; the remaining 24 non-hydrogen-bonded conformers follow, ordered by decreasing residual O6-H7···O10 proximity as a weak tiebreaker, with acknowledged uncertainty in their relative order.

The molecule is a tetrahydrofuran ring (ring atoms C2-C3-C6-O9-C10) bearing a methyl group on C2 and a -CH2-CH(OH)- type side chain (C11-C13-O15-H16) on C10. The dominant conformational feature that differentiates the 30 structures is whether the side-chain hydroxyl (O15-H16) can fold back and form an intramolecular hydrogen bond to the ring ether oxygen (O9), closing a favorable 6-membered pseudo-ring (O9-C10-C11-C13-O15-H16...O9). I measured the H16···O9 distance and the O15-H16···O9 angle in every conformer as the key discriminator.

Seven conformers show a genuine short-range O-H···O contact (~1.98-2.10 Å) with reasonable donor angles (128-140°), indicating a real intramolecular hydrogen bond that stabilizes the structure: 14 (1.98 Å, 139°), 28 (1.98 Å, 139°), 29 (1.98 Å, 139°), 11 (2.00 Å, 140°), 8 (2.01 Å, 134°), 23 (2.10 Å, 128°). Conformer 13 shows a weaker, longer-range interaction (2.58 Å, ~119°) that is only marginally stabilizing. All other conformers have the hydroxyl group pointing away from the ring oxygen, with H···O distances of 3.2 Å or more (up to ~4.9 Å), meaning no intramolecular H-bond is present and the side chain is essentially freely rotated/extended, losing this stabilization (typically worth several kcal/mol in such systems).

Among the non-hydrogen-bonded conformers, I used the residual H16···O9 distance as a weak secondary proxy for partial folding/favorable side-chain rotamer (shorter residual distance suggesting a rotamer closer to, but not quite achieving, the H-bonded geometry, versus fully extended anti conformations that maximize distance and offer no compensating interaction). This secondary ordering (4, 25, 10, 12 showing intermediate distances of 3.2-4.0 Å, followed by the fully extended set at >4.2 Å) is much less certain than the top-tier H-bond ranking, since once the H-bond is broken, other factors (ring pucker, minor eclipsing/gauche H...H contacts) that were not exhaustively analyzed could reorder these structures. I flag this secondary ranking as low-confidence relative ordering, while the top 6-7 H-bonded conformers are ranked with higher confidence based on clear geometric H-bond quality (distance + angle).

The molecule is an acyclic chain CH3–CH(CHO)–CH2–O–CH=NH (a formimidate ester attached through a CH2 to a 2-methyl-propanal-type stereocenter). Connectivity is identical in all 30 files, so differences in energy must come from (1) conformation about the C(central)-C(CHO), C(central)-CH2, and CH2-O single bonds, and (2) the relative orientation of the two polar sp2 groups, the aldehyde C=O and the formimidate C=N(H). 

First I checked whether an intramolecular N–H···O=C hydrogen bond (a 7-membered ring closing C6(=O)-C5-C9-O12-C13=N14-H15) could form. Computing the H15···O7 distances and N–H···O angles for all conformers, the closest approaches (~2.8–3.2 Å, e.g. 15, 24, 3, 4) all have very poor N–H···O angles (60–70° rather than the ~150–180° required for a real H-bond), so no genuine directional H-bond is present in any conformer – this factor can be discarded.

I then checked the O(ether)-C13=N14 conjugation dihedral (C9-O12-C13-N14): in every conformer sampled this stayed close to 0° (syn-planar), confirming that the resonance-stabilized, ester-like O-CH=NH unit is uniformly well-conjugated in all 30 structures and is not a differentiating factor. I also verified the C=N geometry (O12-C13-N14-H15 dihedral, ~178-179° in the examples checked) is the same (trans/E) NH orientation throughout, confirming these are true conformers, not E/Z isomers.

Given the lack of H-bonding and the constancy of the imidate conjugation, the dominant remaining electronic factor is the dipole-dipole interaction between the two polarized π systems, C=O and C=N. I computed the angle between the C6→O7 (carbonyl) vector and the C13→N14 (imine) vector for every conformer. Antiperiplanar/antiparallel alignment (angle near 180°) minimizes unfavorable dipole-dipole repulsion and is stabilizing, whereas near-parallel alignment (angle near 0°) places the two dipoles head-to-tail in a destabilizing arrangement, and near-perpendicular arrangements are roughly neutral.

Results (angle between C=O and C=N vectors): conformer 8 (172°), 23 (169°), 17 (168°), 6 (165°) show the strongest antiparallel alignment (most stabilized); conformers 5 (13°), 18 (17°), 2 (23°), 28 (24°), 25 (26°) show strongly parallel, destabilized dipole alignments. Intermediate/perpendicular conformers (11,12,19,20,22,26,29,9,16) are roughly neutral electrostatically, and are ranked by how close their angle is to the antiparallel optimum. This single, chemically transparent criterion (dipole alignment of the two most polar functional groups) was used as the principal ranking metric, since no H-bonding or ring-strain differences distinguish the conformers and detailed steric (van der Waals) differences are expected to be secondary and are not resolved with high confidence by hand. Thus the ranking below should be viewed as most reliable at the extremes (top few and bottom few) and more uncertain in the closely-spaced middle region where dipole angles cluster near 90-115°.

The molecule (C6H13NO2, open-chain: HOCH2-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH2-NH-CHO, an N-formyl amino alcohol) has no ring, so the dominant stability discriminator is intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl group and either the amide carbonyl oxygen (O-H...O=C, forming an 8-membered pseudo-ring) or the amide N-H and the hydroxyl oxygen (N-H...O-H, forming a 7-membered pseudo-ring), plus general chain compactness/strain in conformers lacking any H-bond. For every conformer I measured (a) the hydroxyl H to carbonyl O distance and (b) the amide N-H to hydroxyl O distance. Short donor-acceptor distances (~1.9-2.1 Å) indicate a genuine, well-oriented intramolecular H-bond; O-H...O=C bonds were treated as slightly stronger than N-H...O-H bonds of the same distance because the alcohol O-H is a better donor and the amide carbonyl O a better acceptor than the amide N-H/alcohol O pair. Conformers 20, 7, 3, 24, 29, 28, 4, 17, 8 and 11 show short, well-formed O-H...O=C contacts (1.87-2.11 Å) and are ranked most stable. Since all 30 files share the same connectivity and the C4=C5 alkene dihedral (checked, ~178-180°) is consistently E in every file, the double-bond geometry is not a discriminating variable; the conformers differ only in rotatable single bonds (C1-C2, C2-O3(H), C2-C4, C5-C6, C6-C7, C6-O8, O8-O9(H)). 

No conformer shows a plausible intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bond: the O3(hydroxyl)···O9(peroxide) heavy-atom distances range from ~4.4 to ~7.0 Å in all structures, and the corresponding O-H···O contact distances are all >4 Å, far outside H-bonding range (<2.5 Å). So H-bonding cannot be used to differentiate stability here.

The most clearly quantifiable, physically well-established conformational effect available in this system is the torsional preference of the peroxide fragment (C6-O8-O9-H21), which behaves like H2O2/alkyl-hydroperoxide torsions: a broad minimum near a gauche dihedral of ~100-115° (lone-pair repulsion minimized), a mild penalty (~1-1.2 kcal/mol) near the anti/eclipsed region (~180°), and a much steeper penalty approaching the fully syn/cis region (~0°, not sampled here). I computed this C-O-O-H dihedral for all 30 conformers via vector/torsion analysis. Values ranged from ~84° (near-ideal gauche) to ~180° (fully anti/eclipsed lone pairs), giving a continuous, chemically meaningful strain ordering. Conformers with dihedral close to 100-120° (e.g. 12, 5, 13, 11, 25, 14, 8, 27, 26) are predicted most stable; those with dihedral collapsing toward the anti extreme (~177-180°, e.g. 18, 6, 29, 17, 28, 7, 3, 19) are predicted least stable, since the anti O-O-C-H arrangement maximizes lone-pair/lone-pair and lone-pair/C-H eclipsing repulsion characteristic of peroxide torsions.

Secondary factors (allylic A^1,3-type strain from the OH/CH3 orientation relative to the alkene at C2, and possible steric clashes between the two methyl groups or between OH and the peroxide chain) were considered but could not be quantified as unambiguously as the peroxide torsion within the time available; they are treated as sources of uncertainty that could shuffle nearby-ranked conformers (especially within the closely clustered ~150-165° and ~177-180° groups, where the numerical differences are small and the ranking there is less certain). No severe short nonbonded clashes (<2.0 Å) were identified in a spot check of the extended chain, so gross steric catastrophes are not expected to reorder the list dramatically.

Overall ranking is therefore built primarily on the peroxide C-O-O-H torsional strain (distance from the ~111° gauche minimum, with an asymmetric penalty function reflecting the shallow anti barrier vs. the steep cis barrier), used as the best available quantitative geometric proxy for relative stability among these conformers.
